advisory.title: Invalid pointer dereference in `fmt::Pointer` impl for `Atomic` and `Shared` when the underlying pointer is invalid
advisory.description: Affected versions of `fmt::Display` dereference the underlying pointer. This causes a invalid pointer dereference e.g., when a pointer created with `Atomic::null` or `Shared::null`. `fmt::Debug` impls and pre-0.9 `fmt::Display` impls, which do not dereference pointers, are not affected by this issue.

advisory.title: Unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in `NsReader` enables memory-exhaustion denial of service
advisory.description:
`NsReader` resolves namespaces by calling `NamespaceResolver::push` for every
`Start`/`Empty` event *before* the event is returned to the caller. `push`
iterated all `xmlns` / `xmlns:*` attributes on the start tag and, for each one,
appended the prefix bytes to an internal buffer and pushed a `NamespaceBinding`
(32 bytes on 64-bit) to an internal `Vec`, with no upper bound on the number of
declarations.

## Impact

A start tag with `N` namespace declarations drove roughly `3×` the tag's byte
size in `NamespaceResolver` heap, allocated *inside* `quick-xml` before the
`NsReader` consumer ever received the event and could inspect or reject it. A
consumer that bounds its *input* size therefore still cannot bound this
allocation: an `M`-byte start tag yields on the order of `3 × M` bytes of
resolver heap the caller never sees.

On untrusted XML this lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker force large heap
allocations with a single start tag. With several `NsReader`s running
concurrently on independent inputs (a common server pattern), the allocations
stack and can exhaust process memory, causing the operating system to kill the
process (OOM). This was confirmed against a real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet
Labs Routinator), where concurrent RRDP validation workers parsing a crafted
`snapshot.xml` exceeded the memory limit and the process was OOM-killed.

## Affected code paths

Consumers using `NsReader` (which always calls `NamespaceResolver::push` before
yielding `Start`/`Empty`), or calling `NamespaceResolver::push` directly. A plain
`Reader` that does not perform namespace resolution is not affected.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`. `NamespaceResolver::push` now rejects a start
tag that declares more than `DEFAULT_MAX_DECLARATIONS_PER_ELEMENT` (256)
namespace bindings, returning the new `NamespaceError::TooManyDeclarations`
instead of allocating without limit. The limit is configurable via
`NamespaceResolver::set_max_declarations_per_element` (use `usize::MAX` to
restore the previous unbounded behavior), and `NsReader::resolver_mut()` is
provided to reach it.

There is no clean workaround for `NsReader` consumers before 0.41.0, as the
allocation happens inside the reader with no configuration knob to cap it.

advisory.title: Quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names
advisory.description:
`BytesStart::attributes()` returns an `Attributes` iterator which, by default
(`with_checks(true)`), rejects a start tag that repeats an attribute name. For
each attribute yielded, the iterator compared the new name against every name
seen so far in the same tag using a linear scan, so a start tag with `N`
distinct attribute names cost `O(N²)` byte comparisons. There was no bound on
`N` other than the size of the buffered start tag.

## Impact

Any code that parses untrusted XML and iterates a start tag's attributes with
the default duplicate check enabled can be made to spend CPU time quadratic in
the number of attributes on a single tag. Because the check is pure computation
with no `.await`/I/O, an I/O-based timeout on the consumer (for example a read
or request timeout) cannot interrupt it while it runs.

Measured cost of a single start tag, release build:

| Attributes on one tag | Time |
|---|---|
| 80,000  | ~6 s   |
| 800,000 | ~10 min |

The cost grows with the square of the attribute count, so a start tag of a few
tens of megabytes can stall a parsing thread for hours. No memory is exhausted
and the parser does not crash; the effect is CPU exhaustion on the thread doing
the parsing: a single crafted start tag can pin a CPU core for minutes to hours,
denying service to that worker. A deployment that places a wall-clock bound on
parsing, or confines it to a non-critical thread, may consider the availability
impact lower.

## Affected code paths

* `BytesStart::attributes()` / `Attributes` iterated with checks enabled (the
  default), and `BytesStart::try_get_attribute`.
* `NsReader`, which resolves namespaces by iterating a tag's attributes and so
  reaches the same check internally.

Consumers that iterate attributes with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` and do
not use `NsReader` are not affected.

This was reported as reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker in a
real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet Labs Routinator) via a crafted RRDP
`snapshot.xml`.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`, where the duplicate check keeps the linear
scan for start tags with a small number of attributes and switches to an `O(1)`
hash pre-filter above a threshold, making the whole tag `O(N)`. The reported
`AttrError::Duplicated` positions are unchanged.

If upgrading is not possible and duplicate-name detection is not required,
disable it with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` (this does not help
`NsReader` consumers, which have no equivalent opt-out before 0.41.0).

advisory.title: Outgoing datagram buffer accounting can panic the sender in quinn-proto
advisory.description:
The limit on memory used to buffer outgoing datagrams, introduced in 0.11.17, subtracted an
evicted datagram's size from the buffered byte counter twice when `Datagrams::send` was called
with `drop = true` (as `Connection::send_datagram` in the `quinn` crate does) while the buffer was
full. Under sustained eviction the counter drifts below its true value: debug builds panic with an
integer underflow, while release builds wrap the counter, drain the whole queue, and then panic on
a desynchronization check in a later `send` call. In `quinn`, this panic occurs while the
connection lock is held, poisoning it and causing a double panic (and thus an abort) when the
connection is dropped.

This can be triggered without a malicious peer, by an application that sends a burst of datagrams
and then idles. It can also be triggered by a peer that keeps the connection alive with PING frames
while withholding acknowledgements, so that the sender's congestion window stays closed and the
outgoing queue never drains. Applications that use `send_datagram_wait` are not affected.

Only 0.11.17 is affected; the flaw was corrected in 0.11.18 by removing the redundant subtraction.

Thanks to [@alexpyattaev](https://github.com/alexpyattaev) for reporting and
[@vcarus](https://github.com/vcarus) for fixing this issue.

advisory.title: Remote peer can panic quinn-proto with zero-length STREAM frames during unordered reads
advisory.description:
When a stream is read in unordered mode (for example through `RecvStream::read(false)` in
quinn-proto or `read_unordered` in `quinn`), quinn-proto proactively deduplicates received data
by recording received ranges in a `RangeSet` through its `replace` method. When an incoming
STREAM frame carried an empty payload, the `Drop` implementation of the iterator returned by
`replace` inserted an empty range into the set, violating the invariant that stored ranges are
non-empty. Subsequent frames overlapping that region then caused a panic while processing the
stream.

A remote peer can trigger this with five small STREAM frames (two of them zero-length) once the
application has put the stream in unordered-read mode. The default ordered read path is not
affected.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.18 by ignoring empty ranges in `RangeSet::replace`.

Thanks to Otto Hermann ([@ojhermann](https://github.com/ojhermann)) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Peer minimum ACK delay can panic quinn-proto when ACK_FREQUENCY transmission is enabled
advisory.description:
When sending ACK_FREQUENCY frames is enabled through
`TransportConfig::ack_frequency_config(Some(..))`, the peer's transport parameters could cause
`AckFrequencyState::candidate_max_ack_delay` to call `Duration::clamp` with a minimum greater
than its maximum, which panics.

For example, a peer advertising a `min_ack_delay` of 100,000 microseconds and a `max_ack_delay`
of 100 milliseconds passes transport parameter validation. At a 5 ms RTT, the lower bound of the
clamp becomes 100 ms while the upper bound is 25 ms, violating the precondition of `clamp` and
panicking while driving the connection. Both automatically derived and explicitly configured
maximum ACK delays use this calculation.

Sending ACK_FREQUENCY frames is disabled by default, so only endpoints that opt in are affected.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.18 by computing the delay with explicit minimum and maximum bounds
instead of `clamp`.

Thanks to [@zerox80](https://github.com/zerox80) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: `Debug` impls for client session values expose TLS secrets
advisory.description:
The `Debug` implementations of `Tls12ClientSessionValue` and
`Tls13ClientSessionValue` were derived, and so included the TLS 1.2 master
secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK in their output.

Custom `ClientSessionStore` implementations that format these values with
`Debug` (for example, when logging) could disclose these secrets to readers of
the logs. This conflicts with rustls's
[key-material redaction policy](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/99f2358cae2954837dbb866faf6727de75489ab9/SECURITY.md#boundary-public-api).

Ordinary connection and built-in session cache `Debug` output is redacted and
is not affected.

advisory.title: Buffered application data sent to outer server after ECH rejection
advisory.description:
When a server rejects Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), the client completes the
handshake using the outer ClientHello and authenticates the server against the
ECH config's `public_name`. At the end of that handshake, rustls encrypted and
queued any application data buffered via `ClientConnection::writer()` *before*
queueing the `ech_required` alert.

The application correctly receives
`Error::PeerIncompatible(ServerRejectedEncryptedClientHello)`, but the next
`write_tls()` call (needed to send the alert) also sends the buffered
application data. Plaintext meant for the inner server therefore goes to the
client-facing server named by `public_name`.

That server is authenticated, so this is not exploitable by an unauthenticated
party, but it violates RFC 9849 section 6.1.6, which requires the client to
abort with `ech_required` "before sending any application data to the server".

This affects only clients that:

- use `EchMode::Enable` (GREASE ECH is not affected),
- write application data before the handshake completes, and
- connect to a server that rejects their ECH config (for example, because it is stale).

The underlying ordering bug is older, but before 0.23.44 the client checked
the server certificate against the inner server name rather than `public_name`,
so certificate verification failed first and no data was sent.

advisory.title: Brotli certificate decompression can allocate up to 1 GiB before authentication
advisory.description:
The built-in Brotli certificate decompressor (enabled by the non-default
`brotli` crate feature) bounded the size of the decompressed output, but
accepted a peer-selected history window. Brotli's large-window extension was
enabled, so a five-byte header could cause an allocation of 1 GiB. A peer can
abort a process whose allocator cannot satisfy that request.

No trusted certificate is required by the attacker. Affected configurations are:

- clients that enable the `brotli` feature and connect to a malicious server, and
- servers that enable the `brotli` feature and request client certificates.

Applications that do not enable the `brotli` feature are not affected.

advisory.title: Unauthenticated ServerHello can downgrade later connections to classical key exchange
advisory.description:
The client recorded the server-selected key exchange group for each server
name when processing the ServerHello, before the server was authenticated.
This record is used to predict which key share to send in future ClientHellos
to that server name.

A network attacker can answer one connection attempt with a ServerHello
selecting X25519, and then close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that
name carry only an X25519 key share, while `supported_groups` still lists
X25519MLKEM768 first. If the genuine server accepts that share rather than
sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake
completes with classical-only key exchange and no error. This persists for as
long as the entry stays in the client's session store.

The impact is loss of post-quantum confidentiality for affected connections
("harvest now, decrypt later"). There is no key compromise and no
authentication bypass.

The following are not affected:

- connections to servers which send a HelloRetryRequest for their preferred group,
- clients with resumption disabled (as nothing is stored), and
- other server names.

This behaviour is discussed in
[draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction-01.html#name-security-considerations),
so the practical impact depends largely on server policy.

advisory.title: Certificate verification may accept distrusted intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys when the configured trust anchors allow such paths.
The private keys corresponding to these intermediates are now well known.

Versions 0.103.16 and 0.104.0-alpha.8 reject paths containing these public keys.

advisory.title: Bundled root certificates allow trust in distrusted emSign intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions include `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, which can allow certificate
paths through distrusted emSign intermediates.

Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys. The private keys corresponding to these intermediates
are now well known.

Version 1.0.10+ removes this root.

Version 0.26.11 is a compatibility wrapper that re-exports
`parent::TLS_SERVER_ROOT_CERTS` from its `webpki-root-certs` 1.x dependency; it
contains no separate root certificate list. Its resolved 1.x dependency must be
updated to 1.0.10 or later.

advisory.title: Bundled root certificates allow trust in distrusted emSign intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions include `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, which can allow certificate
paths through distrusted emSign intermediates.

Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys. The private keys corresponding to these intermediates
are now well known.

Version 1.0.10+ removes this root.

The `webpki-roots` 0.26.11 compatibility package contains no independent trust
store and re-exports the roots from its separately resolved 1.x dependency.
That parent dependency must resolve to 1.0.10 or newer; an older parent remains
affected by this advisory.

advisory.title: async-std has been discontinued
advisory.description:
The `async-std` has been discontinued.

Alternatives:

- [smol](https://crates.io/crates/smol)

advisory.title: core2 is unmaintained, all versions yanked
advisory.description:
The maintainer decided stop maintaining crate and yanked all published versions.

Potential alternatives:

- [`embedded-io`](https://crates.io/crates/embedded-io) solves the same general problem
- [`no-std-io2`](https://crates.io/crates/no-std-io2) is a maintained fork

advisory.title: paste - no longer maintained
advisory.description:
The creator of the crate `paste` has stated in the [`README.md`](https://github.com/dtolnay/paste/blob/master/README.md) 
that this project is not longer maintained as well as archived the repository

## Possible Alternative(s)

- [`pastey`]: a fork of paste and is aimed to be a drop-in replacement with additional features for paste crate
- [`with_builtin_macros`]: crate providing a [superset of `paste`'s functionality including general `macro_rules!` eager expansions](https://docs.rs/with_builtin_macros/0.1.0/with_builtin_macros/macro.with_eager_expansions.html)  and `concat!`/`concat_idents!` macros

[`pastey`]: https://crates.io/crates/pastey
[`with_builtin_macros`]: https://crates.io/crates/with_builtin_macros

advisory.title: rustls-pemfile is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The rustls-pemfile crate is no longer maintained. The repository has been archived since August
2025, and users are encouraged to depend directly on the underlying PEM parsing code included
in rustls-pki-types since 1.9.0. The latest version of rustls-pemfile is in fact a thin wrapper
around the same code used in rustls-pki-types, so migrating should be straightforward.

The new API is represented by the [`PemObject`][PemObject] trait, which provides methods for
reading a single or multiple PEM objects from a file or byte slice.

[PemObject]: https://docs.rs/rustls-pki-types/latest/rustls_pki_types/pem/trait.PemObject.html

advisory.title: `rustybuzz` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The current maintainer of `rustybuzz` has stated that the crate is unmaintained and will not receive further fixes or updates (see the referenced issue).

## Alternative(s)

- [`harfrust`](https://github.com/harfbuzz/harfrust), an actively maintained and updated alternative which is part of the Harfbuzz project.

advisory.title: `ttf-parser` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The author of `ttf-parser` has stated that the crate is unmaintained and will not receive further fixes (see the referenced issue).

## Alternative(s)

- [`skrifa`](https://crates.io/crates/skrifa), an actively maintained TrueType and OpenType font parsing crate, part of the Google Fonts "oxidize" (`fontations`) project.

advisory.title: unsafe-libyaml is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The [repository](https://github.com/dtolnay/unsafe-libyaml) was archived by
its owner on 2024-03-25 and is read-only. The last release is 0.2.11
(March 2024).

`unsafe-libyaml` is a machine translation of libyaml's C code into unsafe
Rust (c2rust). Bugs found in it will not be fixed upstream. It is used by
`serde_yaml` (itself deprecated) and by forks such as `serde_yaml_ng`.

## Alternatives

Consider a YAML parser written in safe Rust, for example:

- [saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/saphyr) ([serde-saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/serde-saphyr) for serde users)
- [noyalib](https://crates.io/crates/noyalib)

advisory.title: `zbus_names` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zbus_names` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `names` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus name types.

advisory.title: `zvariant` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zvariant` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `wire` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format. Users of the GVariant format should migrate to [`zgvariant`](https://crates.io/crates/zgvariant).

advisory.title: `zvariant_derive` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zvariant_derive` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

Its derive macros are provided by [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format.

advisory.title: `event-listener` allows `!Send` tags to cross thread boundaries via `StackSlot`
advisory.description:
Affected versions of `event-listener` unconditionally implement `Send` and
`Sync` for `StackSlot<'_, T>`, the stack-allocated listener type created
by the `listener!` macro.

This allows a `!Send` tag type set via `Event::with_tag` to be moved to
another thread and accessed via `StackSlot::wait`, causing a data race in safe
code.

advisory.title: Unchecked pointer offset in crate `memmap2`
advisory.description:
Affected versionf of `memmap2` did not perform enough validation on the `offset` and `len` parameters of
`Mmap::[unchecked_]advise_range()`,
`MmapMut::[unchecked_]advise_ranage()`
and `MmapMut::flush[_async]_range()`.

This can cause undefined behavior due to invalid values being passed to [`pointer::offset()`] and [`pointer::add()`]
when passing an out-of-bounds range to any of the affected functions.

The flaw was corrected in commit [`cee7cf0`] and released in version `0.9.11`.

The invalid pointer is not dereferenced,
but it is passed to the `madvise` and `msync` syscalls and their Windows equivalents.

[`pointer::offset()`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/primitive.pointer.html#method.offset-1
[`pointer::add()`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/primitive.pointer.html#method.add-1
[`cee7cf0`] https://github.com/RazrFalcon/memmap2-rs/pull/170/changes/cee7cf03a9ee095982a3c37b7aac8e3f68f1a00c
